title: linux-drives
description: Complete lifecycle of storage device management on Linux: identifying disks, partitioning, formatting, mounting, unmounting, persisting mounts, LUKS encryption, LVM, swap, and filesystem maintenance. Examples use Arch Linux tooling.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
This guide covers the full lifecycle of storage device management on Linux: identifying disks, partitioning, formatting, mounting, encrypting, and safely removing them. Examples use Arch Linux tooling (`pacman`, `systemd`), but the underlying commands (`lsblk`, `mount`, `mkfs`, `cryptsetup`) are the same across nearly every distro.

## Core concepts

Linux represents storage as **block devices** under `/dev`:

| Device | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `/dev/sda` | First SATA/SCSI/USB disk (whole disk) |
| `/dev/sda1` | First partition on that disk |
| `/dev/nvme0n1` | First NVMe disk |
| `/dev/nvme0n1p1` | First partition on that NVMe disk |
| `/dev/mapper/foo` | A device-mapper node — LUKS-decrypted volumes and LVM logical volumes appear here |

A **partition** is a labeled region of a disk. A **filesystem** (ext4, btrfs, xfs, vfat, ...) is a structure written *inside* a partition (or, less commonly, directly on a whole disk) that lets the kernel store files. **Mounting** attaches a filesystem to a directory (a *mount point*) so you can access it; **unmounting** detaches it.

## Install the tools

On Arch, most of what you need is already in `util-linux` (installed by default). A few extras:

```bash
sudo pacman -S parted gptfdisk dosfstools e2fsprogs cryptsetup lvm2 btrfs-progs ntfs-3g
```

| Package | Provides |
| --- | --- |
| `parted` / `gptfdisk` | Partitioning tools (`parted`, `gdisk`) |
| `dosfstools` | `mkfs.fat` / `mkfs.vfat` for FAT32 |
| `e2fsprogs` | `mkfs.ext4`, `e2fsck`, etc. |
| `cryptsetup` | LUKS disk encryption |
| `lvm2` | Logical Volume Manager |
| `btrfs-progs` | Btrfs tools |
| `ntfs-3g` | Read/write NTFS (Windows filesystems) |

## List and identify devices

This is the command you'll run before touching any disk — always confirm the device name first:

```bash
lsblk
```

```text
NAME        MAJ:MIN RM   SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINTS
sda           8:0    0 465.8G  0 disk
├─sda1        8:1    0   512M  0 part /boot
└─sda2        8:2    0 465.2G  0 part /
sdb           8:16   1  57.6G  0 disk
└─sdb1        8:17   1  57.6G  0 part
nvme0n1     259:0    0 931.5G  0 disk
```

Useful variants:

```bash
lsblk -f          # show filesystem type, label, UUID
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT,UUID
sudo blkid        # list filesystems with UUIDs directly
sudo fdisk -l      # low-level listing, including unpartitioned disks
```

**Rule of thumb: before any destructive command, run `lsblk` and confirm the exact device path.** Getting this wrong (e.g. `sda` instead of `sdb`) can wipe your system disk.

Next: [Understanding Filesystems](/linux-drives/understanding-filesystems/).
Getting Started.Understanding Filesystems:
Before formatting anything, it helps to know what you're choosing between.

## Common filesystems

| Filesystem | Typical use | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **ext4** | Linux root/home, general purpose | Mature, stable, the long-time Linux default |
| **btrfs** | Linux root, snapshots | Copy-on-write, built-in snapshots and subvolumes |
| **xfs** | Large files, servers | Good large-file/parallel I/O performance |
| **vfat / FAT32** | USB drives, EFI system partition | Max file size 4GB, universally readable (Windows/macOS/Linux) |
| **exFAT** | Large USB/SD drives | Like FAT32 but no 4GB file limit; cross-platform |
| **NTFS** | Windows drives | Read/write via `ntfs-3g`; not ideal as a Linux root fs |
| **swap** | Virtual memory | Not a general filesystem — holds swapped-out RAM pages |

## Partition tables: MBR vs GPT

Before a disk has filesystems, it needs a **partition table** describing where partitions live.

| | MBR (msdos) | GPT |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Max disk size | 2TB | Effectively unlimited |
| Max partitions | 4 primary (or 3 + extended) | 128 by default |
| UEFI boot | Not natively supported | Required for UEFI boot |
| Recommendation | Legacy/BIOS systems only | Use this for anything new |

On a modern Arch install, use **GPT**. You'll see it referred to as `gpt` in `parted` and as the default in `gdisk`.

## The EFI System Partition (ESP)

If your system boots via UEFI (nearly all modern hardware), you need a small **FAT32** partition, typically mounted at `/boot` or `/efi`, flagged as the ESP. This is where the bootloader lives. It's usually 300MB–1GB and created once during OS installation — see [Learn by Using](/linux-drives/learn-01-adding-a-new-disk/) for a full example.

## Choosing a filesystem in practice

- **Root/home on Linux**: ext4 (safe default) or btrfs (if you want snapshots).
- **External/USB drive shared with Windows or macOS**: exFAT.
- **USB drive Linux-only**: ext4.
- **EFI system partition**: always FAT32 — this is a firmware requirement, not a preference.
- **Swap**: dedicated swap partition, or a swap file (see [Swap](/linux-drives/swap/)).

Next: [Partitioning](/linux-drives/partitioning/).

Essential Commands.Partitioning:
Partitioning divides a raw disk into labeled regions. Two common tools: `parted` (scriptable, works with both MBR and GPT) and `gdisk` (GPT-focused, interactive).

**This is a destructive operation.** Always confirm the device with `lsblk` first.

## View existing partitions

```bash
sudo parted /dev/sdb print
sudo gdisk /dev/sdb -l
```

## Create a GPT partition table (wipes the disk)

```bash
sudo parted /dev/sdb mklabel gpt
```

## Create a partition with parted

```bash
sudo parted /dev/sdb mkpart primary ext4 0% 100%
```

| Argument | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `primary` | Partition type label (GPT doesn't really distinguish primary/logical, but parted still asks) |
| `ext4` | Filesystem hint (parted does NOT format — this is just a label) |
| `0% 100%` | Start and end — using percentages lets parted pick aligned boundaries |

For a specific size instead of percentages:

```bash
sudo parted /dev/sdb mkpart primary ext4 1MiB 20GiB
```

## Create a partition with gdisk (interactive)

```bash
sudo gdisk /dev/sdb
```

Inside gdisk:

```text
Command: n        # new partition
Partition number: 1
First sector:      (press Enter for default)
Last sector:       +20G
Hex code:          8300   (Linux filesystem) or 8200 (Linux swap), EF00 (EFI system)
Command: w         # write and exit
```

## Common gdisk hex codes

| Code | Type |
| --- | --- |
| `8300` | Linux filesystem |
| `8200` | Linux swap |
| `EF00` | EFI System Partition |
| `8e00` | Linux LVM |
| `8309` | Linux LUKS |

## Delete a partition

```bash
sudo parted /dev/sdb rm 1
```

## Verify

```bash
lsblk /dev/sdb
sudo parted /dev/sdb print
```

The kernel sometimes needs a nudge to notice partition table changes:

```bash
sudo partprobe /dev/sdb
```

Next: [Formatting](/linux-drives/formatting/).
Essential Commands.Formatting:
Formatting writes a filesystem structure onto a partition (or whole disk). This is also destructive — it erases existing data on that partition.

## ext4

```bash
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1
sudo mkfs.ext4 -L mydata /dev/sdb1     # with a label
```

## Btrfs

```bash
sudo mkfs.btrfs /dev/sdb1
sudo mkfs.btrfs -L mydata /dev/sdb1
```

## XFS

```bash
sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/sdb1
sudo mkfs.xfs -L mydata /dev/sdb1
```

## FAT32 (USB drives, EFI partition)

```bash
sudo mkfs.fat -F32 /dev/sdb1
sudo mkfs.fat -F32 -n MYUSB /dev/sdb1
```

`-F32` forces FAT32 (vs FAT12/16). Required for the EFI System Partition.

## exFAT

```bash
sudo mkfs.exfat -n mydata /dev/sdb1
```

## Swap

```bash
sudo mkswap /dev/sdb2
```

(See [Swap](/linux-drives/swap/) for enabling it afterward.)

## Flag reference

| Flag (common across mkfs.*) | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `-L label` / `-n label` | Volume label (`-n` for fat/exfat, `-L` for ext4/btrfs/xfs) |
| `-F` | Force (skip "are you sure" prompts / override type detection for fat) |

## Verify the format

```bash
lsblk -f /dev/sdb1
sudo blkid /dev/sdb1
```

```text
/dev/sdb1: LABEL="mydata" UUID="a1b2c3d4-..." TYPE="ext4"
```

Next: [Mounting and Unmounting](/linux-drives/mounting-and-unmounting/).
Essential Commands.Mounting and Unmounting:
Mounting attaches a filesystem to a directory so the kernel exposes its contents there. Unmounting detaches it cleanly.

## Manual mount

```bash
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/mydata
sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/mydata
```

Mount with explicit options:

```bash
sudo mount -o rw,noatime /dev/sdb1 /mnt/mydata
```

| Option | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `rw` / `ro` | Read-write (default) or read-only |
| `noatime` | Don't update file access timestamps (small perf gain) |
| `uid=1000,gid=1000` | For FAT/NTFS — set file ownership, since those filesystems don't have Linux permissions |
| `defaults` | rw, suid, dev, exec, auto, nouser, async — the standard baseline |

Mounting a FAT/exFAT drive so your own user owns the files:

```bash
sudo mount -o uid=$(id -u),gid=$(id -g) /dev/sdb1 /mnt/mydata
```

## Mount by UUID or label

More reliable than device names, which can shift between boots:

```bash
sudo mount UUID=a1b2c3d4-... /mnt/mydata
sudo mount LABEL=mydata /mnt/mydata
```

## View current mounts

```bash
mount | grep sdb1
findmnt /dev/sdb1
lsblk
```

## Unmount

```bash
sudo umount /mnt/mydata
# or by device:
sudo umount /dev/sdb1
```

## "Target is busy" — force it

If unmounting fails because something's using the filesystem:

```bash
# find what's using it
sudo fuser -vm /mnt/mydata
sudo lsof +D /mnt/mydata

# then close those processes, or as a last resort:
sudo umount -l /mnt/mydata    # lazy unmount — detaches once no longer busy
sudo umount -f /mnt/mydata    # force (mainly useful for unresponsive NFS)
```

Prefer closing the offending process over `-l`/`-f` when possible — lazy/force unmounts can leave writes incomplete.

## Safely removing a USB drive

```bash
sudo umount /dev/sdb1
sudo eject /dev/sdb        # optional, spins down/signals safe removal
```

Always unmount before physically disconnecting — otherwise buffered writes may never make it to disk.

Next: [Persistent Mounts with fstab](/linux-drives/fstab/).
Essential Commands.Persistent Mounts with fstab:
A manual `mount` doesn't survive a reboot. `/etc/fstab` defines mounts that happen automatically at boot.

## Get the UUID first

Always use UUIDs in fstab, not `/dev/sdX` names — device letters can change between boots (e.g. if you add/remove a drive).

```bash
sudo blkid /dev/sdb1
```

```text
/dev/sdb1: LABEL="mydata" UUID="a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-1234567890ab" TYPE="ext4"
```

## Edit /etc/fstab

```bash
sudo nano /etc/fstab
```

Each line has 6 fields:

```text
UUID=a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-1234567890ab  /mnt/mydata  ext4  defaults,noatime  0  2
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Device | `UUID=...` (preferred) or `LABEL=...` or `/dev/sdb1` |
| 2. Mount point | Directory (must already exist) |
| 3. Filesystem type | `ext4`, `btrfs`, `vfat`, `swap`, etc. |
| 4. Options | Comma-separated, no spaces |
| 5. Dump | Almost always `0` (legacy backup flag) |
| 6. Pass | fsck order: `0` = skip, `1` = root filesystem, `2` = everything else |

## Example entries

```text
# Internal ext4 drive
UUID=a1b2c3d4-...  /mnt/mydata     ext4   defaults,noatime          0  2

# EFI system partition
UUID=1234-ABCD     /boot           vfat   defaults,noatime          0  2

# External FAT32 USB (owned by user 1000)
UUID=5678-EFGH     /mnt/usb        vfat   defaults,uid=1000,gid=1000,umask=022  0  2

# Swap
UUID=9abc-def0-...  none           swap   sw                        0  0
```

## Test before rebooting

Never reboot immediately after editing fstab without testing — a broken fstab entry for a critical mount point can make the system fail to boot.

```bash
sudo mount -a
```

This mounts everything in fstab that isn't already mounted. If it errors, fix the line before rebooting.

## Removable/optional drives

For a USB drive that isn't always connected, add `nofail` so boot doesn't hang waiting for it:

```text
UUID=5678-EFGH  /mnt/usb  vfat  defaults,nofail,x-systemd.automount  0  2
```

`x-systemd.automount` mounts it on first access instead of at boot, which pairs well with `nofail`.

Next: [Disk Encryption with LUKS](/linux-drives/luks-encryption/).

## nofail and boot delay

By itself, `nofail` prevents boot from *failing* if the drive is absent — but the default device wait is 90 seconds, so a disconnected drive can still make boot noticeably slower. Pair `nofail` with an explicit timeout:

```text
UUID=5678-EFGH  /mnt/usb  vfat  defaults,nofail,x-systemd.device-timeout=5,x-systemd.automount  0  2
```

`x-systemd.device-timeout=5` caps the wait at 5 seconds instead of 90. Don't set it to `0` — that means infinite, the opposite of what you want.
Essential Commands.Disk Encryption with LUKS:
LUKS (Linux Unified Key Setup) is the standard full-disk/partition encryption scheme on Linux, implemented via `cryptsetup`.

## How it fits into the stack

```text
[ disk partition ] → [ LUKS encryption layer ] → [ /dev/mapper/name ] → [ filesystem ] → [ mount point ]
```

You format the *raw partition* as LUKS, then the *decrypted* mapped device gets a normal filesystem on top.

## Encrypt a partition

**This destroys existing data on the partition.**

```bash
sudo cryptsetup luksFormat /dev/sdb1
```

You'll be prompted to type `YES` (uppercase, exactly) and set a passphrase. Use a strong passphrase — this is the only thing standing between someone with the disk and your data.

## Open (unlock) the encrypted partition

```bash
sudo cryptsetup open /dev/sdb1 mydata
```

This creates `/dev/mapper/mydata` after you enter the passphrase. The name (`mydata`) is arbitrary — pick something memorable.

## Format the decrypted volume

Now format *the mapped device*, not the raw partition:

```bash
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/mapper/mydata
```

## Mount it

```bash
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/mydata
sudo mount /dev/mapper/mydata /mnt/mydata
```

## Unmount and close, when done

```bash
sudo umount /mnt/mydata
sudo cryptsetup close mydata
```

After `close`, `/dev/mapper/mydata` disappears and the underlying partition is unreadable without the passphrase again.

## Automating unlock at boot (optional)

For a drive you want auto-unlocked at boot (e.g. via a keyfile, not recommended for removable drives you might lose):

```bash
# generate a keyfile
sudo dd if=/dev/urandom of=/root/mydata.key bs=512 count=4
sudo chmod 600 /root/mydata.key
sudo cryptsetup luksAddKey /dev/sdb1 /root/mydata.key
```

Then reference it in `/etc/crypttab`:

```text
mydata  UUID=a1b2c3d4-...  /root/mydata.key  luks
```

And in `/etc/fstab`, mount the mapped device as usual:

```text
/dev/mapper/mydata  /mnt/mydata  ext4  defaults,noatime  0  2
```

**Caution:** a keyfile stored on the same unencrypted boot disk protects against a stolen *external* drive, but not against someone with access to the machine itself. For a laptop's root filesystem, full-disk LUKS with passphrase entry at boot (set up during OS installation) is the standard approach.

## Manage passphrases

```bash
sudo cryptsetup luksAddKey /dev/sdb1        # add another passphrase/keyfile
sudo cryptsetup luksRemoveKey /dev/sdb1     # remove one
sudo cryptsetup luksDump /dev/sdb1          # show key slots and metadata
```

`cryptsetup luksFormat` uses **LUKS2** by default on current versions (Arch's `cryptsetup` package), with `argon2id` as the key derivation function — a memory-hard KDF that's significantly more resistant to hardware-accelerated brute force than LUKS1's `pbkdf2`. You don't need to pass any extra flags to get this; it's already the default. If you specifically need LUKS1 (e.g. for compatibility with an older bootloader or GRUB config that doesn't support LUKS2), format with `--type luks1` explicitly.

LUKS1 supports up to 8 key slots; **LUKS2 supports up to 32** — useful for e.g. a personal passphrase, a recovery keyfile, and a TPM-bound key all at once.

Essential Commands.Logical Volume Management:
LVM adds a flexible layer between raw partitions and filesystems: you can combine disks into a pool and carve out resizable volumes, independent of physical partition boundaries.

## The three layers

```text
Physical Volumes (PVs) → Volume Group (VG) → Logical Volumes (LVs)
   /dev/sdb1, /dev/sdc1  →      vg_data       →   lv_data, lv_backup
```

## Create physical volumes

```bash
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
sudo pvs                              # list PVs
```

## Create a volume group

```bash
sudo vgcreate vg_data /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
sudo vgs
sudo vgdisplay vg_data
```

## Create logical volumes

```bash
sudo lvcreate -L 50G -n lv_data vg_data
sudo lvcreate -l 100%FREE -n lv_backup vg_data   # use all remaining space
sudo lvs
```

`-L` sets an absolute size (`50G`), `-l` sets it as a percentage or extent count.

## Format and mount like any partition

Logical volumes appear at `/dev/vg_data/lv_data` (or `/dev/mapper/vg_data-lv_data`):

```bash
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/vg_data/lv_data
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/data
sudo mount /dev/vg_data/lv_data /mnt/data
```

## Resize a logical volume

Grow it (filesystem resize covered on [Resizing Filesystems](/linux-drives/resizing/)):

```bash
sudo lvextend -L +20G /dev/vg_data/lv_data
sudo resize2fs /dev/vg_data/lv_data    # for ext4, after extending
```

Shrinking is riskier — always shrink the filesystem *before* shrinking the LV, and back up first.

## Remove (in order: LV, then VG, then PV)

```bash
sudo umount /mnt/data
sudo lvremove /dev/vg_data/lv_data
sudo vgremove vg_data
sudo pvremove /dev/sdb1
```

## When to reach for LVM vs plain partitions

| Use plain partitions when | Use LVM when |
| --- | --- |
| Simple single-disk setup | You want to resize volumes without repartitioning |
| You know sizes won't change | You want to combine multiple disks into one pool |
| Minimal complexity desired | You want to take LVM snapshots |

Btrfs subvolumes offer similar flexibility to LVM+ext4 with less layering, if you're choosing a setup from scratch.

Next: [Swap](/linux-drives/swap/).
Essential Commands.Swap:
Swap gives the kernel disk space to use as overflow when RAM is full. It can be a dedicated partition or a file.

## Swap partition

Format a partition (see [Formatting](/linux-drives/formatting/)) as swap and enable it:

```bash
sudo mkswap /dev/sdb2
sudo swapon /dev/sdb2
```

Make it persistent via `/etc/fstab`:

```text
UUID=9abc-def0-...  none  swap  sw  0  0
```

## Swap file (no dedicated partition needed)

```bash
sudo fallocate -l 4G /swapfile
sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
sudo mkswap /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile
```

If `fallocate` isn't supported by your filesystem (some btrfs configs need special handling):

```bash
sudo dd if=/dev/zero of=/swapfile bs=1M count=4096 status=progress
```

Persist it in `/etc/fstab`:

```text
/swapfile  none  swap  sw  0  0
```

## Check swap status

```bash
swapon --show
free -h
```

```text
               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:            15Gi       4.2Gi       8.1Gi       412Mi       3.0Gi        10Gi
Swap:          4.0Gi          0B        4.0Gi
```

## Disable swap

```bash
sudo swapoff /dev/sdb2
sudo swapoff /swapfile
```

Remove the corresponding line from `/etc/fstab` if you don't want it back at next boot.

## How much swap?

| RAM | Typical swap (general desktop use) |
| --- | --- |
| ≤ 8GB | Equal to RAM, or more if using hibernation |
| 8–32GB | 4–8GB, or = RAM if hibernating |
| 32GB+ | A few GB is often enough unless hibernating |

If you use **hibernation** (suspend-to-disk), swap must be at least as large as your RAM.

Next: [Checking and Repairing Filesystems](/linux-drives/fsck-and-repair/).
Essential Commands.Checking and Repairing Filesystems:
Filesystems can develop errors from unclean shutdowns, failing hardware, or bugs. `fsck` (filesystem check) tools detect and repair these.

## Golden rule: never fsck a mounted filesystem

Checking (especially repairing) a mounted filesystem can cause corruption. Unmount first, or check from a live USB/rescue environment if it's your root filesystem.

```bash
sudo umount /dev/sdb1
```

## ext4

```bash
sudo e2fsck -f /dev/sdb1          # -f forces a check even if it looks clean
sudo e2fsck -fy /dev/sdb1         # -y auto-answers "yes" to repair prompts
```

## Generic wrapper (dispatches based on filesystem type)

```bash
sudo fsck /dev/sdb1
sudo fsck -A                       # check everything listed in fstab
```

## Btrfs

Btrfs handles many errors via self-healing (if using RAID1/DUP metadata) and scrubbing rather than a traditional fsck:

```bash
sudo btrfs scrub start /mnt/mydata
sudo btrfs scrub status /mnt/mydata
sudo btrfs check /dev/sdb1        # read-only check; unmount first
```

Avoid `btrfs check --repair` unless guided by documentation or support — it can make things worse if misused.

## XFS

```bash
sudo xfs_repair /dev/sdb1
```

XFS cannot be checked with the filesystem mounted read-write; unmount first.

## Checking your root filesystem

You generally can't unmount `/`. Options:
- Boot from a live USB and run `fsck` on the unmounted partition.
- For ext4, schedule a check on next boot: `sudo touch /forcefsck` (checked at next startup on some setups), or use `tune2fs -c 1 /dev/sdaX` to force periodic checks.

## Checking SMART health (hardware-level, not filesystem)

```bash
sudo pacman -S smartmontools
sudo smartctl -a /dev/sda
sudo smartctl -H /dev/sda    # quick health summary
```

This checks the physical drive's self-reported health — worth running periodically, especially before trusting a drive with important data.

Next: [Resizing Filesystems](/linux-drives/resizing/).
Essential Commands.Resizing Filesystems:
Growing or shrinking a filesystem safely means keeping the partition (or LV) size and the filesystem size in sync, and always going partition-then-filesystem when growing, filesystem-then-partition when shrinking.

## Grow: partition/LV first, filesystem second

**Growing a partition with parted:**

```bash
sudo umount /dev/sdb1
sudo parted /dev/sdb resizepart 1 100%
```

**Then grow the filesystem to fill it:**

```bash
# ext4
sudo e2fsck -f /dev/sdb1
sudo resize2fs /dev/sdb1

# btrfs (can be done mounted, online)
sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/mydata
sudo btrfs filesystem resize max /mnt/mydata

# xfs (can only grow, and only while mounted)
sudo xfs_growfs /mnt/mydata
```

**Growing an LVM logical volume + ext4 in one step:**

```bash
sudo lvextend -r -L +20G /dev/vg_data/lv_data
```

`-r` tells `lvextend` to resize the filesystem automatically afterward (supported for ext4/xfs).

## Shrink: filesystem first, partition second

Shrinking is the reverse order, and only some filesystems support it at all.

```bash
# ext4 — unmount first, shrink fs, then shrink partition
sudo umount /dev/sdb1
sudo e2fsck -f /dev/sdb1
sudo resize2fs /dev/sdb1 20G
sudo parted /dev/sdb resizepart 1 20GiB
```

**XFS cannot be shrunk at all** — only grown. If you need a smaller XFS filesystem, you must back up, recreate it smaller, and restore.

**Btrfs can shrink online:**

```bash
sudo btrfs filesystem resize -5G /mnt/mydata
```

## Before any resize: back up

Resizing carries real risk of data loss, especially shrinking. Back up first, and prefer growing over shrinking when you have a choice — growing is inherently safer since you're not discarding blocks that might contain data.

## Verify afterward

```bash
lsblk
df -h /mnt/mydata
sudo e2fsck -f /dev/sdb1   # ext4: verify integrity post-resize
```

Next, see the full lifecycle applied together in [Learn by Using](/linux-drives/learn-01-adding-a-new-disk/).

Project.FAQ:
### Why use UUIDs instead of /dev/sdX in fstab?

Device names like `/dev/sdb` are assigned by enumeration order at boot, which can change if you add, remove, or reorder USB devices. UUIDs are generated once when a filesystem is created and never change, so they're the reliable choice for anything persistent.

### What's the difference between the LUKS partition UUID and the filesystem UUID?

They're two different UUIDs on two different layers. `blkid /dev/sda1` (the raw partition) shows the **LUKS container's** UUID, used in `/etc/crypttab`. `blkid /dev/mapper/name` (the decrypted mapped device) shows the **filesystem's** UUID, used in `/etc/fstab`. Mixing these up is a common source of confusing fstab errors.

### Is LUKS2 the default now?

Yes — current `cryptsetup` uses LUKS2 by default for `luksFormat`, with `argon2id` as the key derivation function. You don't need to pass `--type luks2` explicitly; it's already the default. See [Disk Encryption with LUKS](/linux-drives/luks-encryption/).

### My drive shows up as /dev/sdb sometimes and /dev/sdc other times — is that a problem?

Not for anything referenced by UUID or LABEL in fstab/crypttab — those don't care what the kernel currently calls the device. It only matters for manual, one-off commands, which is why this guide always says to check with `lsblk` immediately before any destructive command.

### Can I resize an encrypted LUKS partition?

Yes, but order matters and it's more involved than resizing a plain partition: grow the underlying partition first, then `cryptsetup resize <name>` to grow the LUKS container to fill it, then resize the filesystem inside. Shrinking reverses that order. Always back up first.

### Do I need to fsck an SSD the same way as an HDD?

The filesystem-level checks (`e2fsck`, `xfs_repair`, etc.) work the same regardless of underlying media. What differs is wear-related maintenance — SSDs benefit from TRIM (`fstrim`, or the `discard` mount option) rather than defragmentation, which is unnecessary and mildly harmful on flash storage.

### What's the quickest way to see what's mounted right now?

```bash
findmnt
```

It shows the full mount tree with sources and options, and is easier to read than raw `mount` output for anything beyond a single device.

Project.Troubleshooting:
Common problems and what they usually mean.

## "mount: /mnt/x: wrong fs type, bad option, bad superblock"

Usually means one of:
- The device path is wrong (double-check with `lsblk`).
- You're trying to mount the raw LUKS partition instead of the decrypted `/dev/mapper/...` device.
- The filesystem is actually corrupted — try `sudo blkid /dev/sdX1` to confirm it's even recognized as a filesystem.

## "umount: target is busy"

Something (a shell `cd`'d into it, an open file, a running process) is still using the mount point.

```bash
sudo fuser -vm /mnt/point
sudo lsof +D /mnt/point
```

Close those, then unmount normally. Avoid `-l`/`-f` unless necessary — see [Mounting and Unmounting](/linux-drives/mounting-and-unmounting/).

## Drive doesn't show up in lsblk at all

- Check `dmesg | tail -40` right after plugging it in — hardware/USB errors show up there.
- Try a different cable/port — especially for USB drives, cable issues are common.
- Check `sudo smartctl -a /dev/sdX` if the drive is detected but behaving oddly — could indicate failing hardware.

## System hangs at boot after editing fstab

A bad fstab entry for a mount without `nofail` can block boot. Boot into a rescue shell (most systemd-based systems offer this automatically, or use a live USB), remount root read-write if needed, and fix or comment out the offending line:

```bash
mount -o remount,rw /
nano /etc/fstab
```

This is exactly why [Persistent Mounts with fstab](/linux-drives/fstab/) recommends testing with `sudo mount -a` before rebooting.

## Forgot a LUKS passphrase

There's no recovery path by design — if you don't have a backup keyslot or keyfile, the data is unrecoverable. This is the tradeoff for genuinely strong encryption. Always set up at least one backup key (`cryptsetup luksAddKey`) when you first encrypt something important.

## "Structure needs cleaning" errors

This indicates filesystem corruption. Unmount immediately and run the appropriate check tool — see [Checking and Repairing Filesystems](/linux-drives/fsck-and-repair/). Don't keep writing to a filesystem showing this error.

Learn by Examples.1. Identifying the New Disk:
You've just plugged in a new external SSD via USB. Before doing anything, find out exactly which device it is.

## Before plugging in

```bash
lsblk
```

```text
NAME        MAJ:MIN RM   SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINTS
nvme0n1     259:0    0 931.5G  0 disk
├─nvme0n1p1 259:1    0   512M  0 part /boot
└─nvme0n1p2 259:2    0   931G  0 part /
```

Just the internal NVMe drive — no `sda` yet.

## After plugging in

```bash
lsblk
```

```text
NAME        MAJ:MIN RM   SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINTS
nvme0n1     259:0    0 931.5G  0 disk
├─nvme0n1p1 259:1    0   512M  0 part /boot
└─nvme0n1p2 259:2    0   931G  0 part /
sda           8:0    1 465.8G  0 disk
```

`sda` appeared — 465.8GB (the "500GB" marketing size), no partitions (`TYPE disk` with no children), not mounted. This is our new drive.

## Double-check with more detail

```bash
sudo fdisk -l /dev/sda
```

```text
Disk /dev/sda: 465.8 GiB, 500107862016 bytes, 976773168 sectors
Disk model: External SSD
...
```

The model name (`External SSD`) confirms it — this matches what we just plugged in, not our internal NVMe.

**This confirmation step matters.** If you skip it and run partitioning commands against the wrong device, you can destroy your OS install. Always re-run `lsblk` right before any destructive command, especially if time has passed or you've plugged/unplugged multiple things.

Next: [Partitioning It](/linux-drives/learn-02-partitioning-it/).
Learn by Examples.2. Partitioning It:
`/dev/sda` is blank. Let's give it a GPT partition table and a single partition spanning the whole disk.

## Create the GPT table

```bash
sudo parted /dev/sda mklabel gpt
```

```text
Warning: The existing disk label on /dev/sda will be destroyed and all data on
this disk will be lost. Do you want to continue?
Yes/No? Yes
```

## Create one partition using the full disk

```bash
sudo parted /dev/sda mkpart primary 0% 100%
```

We didn't specify a filesystem type hint here because this partition is going to hold LUKS, not a filesystem directly — `parted` won't be formatting it anyway.

## Confirm

```bash
lsblk /dev/sda
```

```text
NAME    MAJ:MIN RM   SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINTS
sda       8:0    1 465.8G  0 disk
└─sda1    8:1    1 465.8G  0 part
```

```bash
sudo parted /dev/sda print
```

```text
Model: External SSD (scsi)
Disk /dev/sda: 500GB
Partition Table: gpt

Number  Start   End    Size   File system  Name     Flags
 1      1049kB  500GB  500GB               primary
```

`/dev/sda1` exists, spans the whole disk, and has no filesystem yet — exactly what we want before encrypting it.

Next: [Encrypting It with LUKS](/linux-drives/learn-03-encrypting-it/).
Learn by Examples.3. Encrypting It with LUKS:
Since this will hold backups, we want it encrypted — if the drive is ever lost or stolen, the data is unreadable without the passphrase.

## Format the partition as LUKS

```bash
sudo cryptsetup luksFormat /dev/sda1
```

```text
WARNING!
========
This will overwrite data on /dev/sda1 irrevocably.

Are you sure? (Type 'yes' in capital letters): YES
Enter passphrase for /dev/sda1:
Verify passphrase:
```

Use a strong, memorable passphrase — there's no recovery option if you forget it and don't have a backup key.

## Open it

```bash
sudo cryptsetup open /dev/sda1 backup_ssd
```

```text
Enter passphrase for /dev/sda1:
```

`backup_ssd` is a name we chose — it'll show up as `/dev/mapper/backup_ssd`.

## Confirm the mapped device exists

```bash
lsblk /dev/sda
```

```text
NAME             MAJ:MIN RM   SIZE RO TYPE  MOUNTPOINTS
sda                8:0    1 465.8G  0 disk
└─sda1             8:1    1 465.8G  0 part
  └─backup_ssd   254:0    0 465.8G  0 crypt
```

The `crypt` type row confirms it: `/dev/mapper/backup_ssd` is the decrypted view of `/dev/sda1`. Everything from here on (formatting, mounting) targets `/dev/mapper/backup_ssd`, not `/dev/sda1` directly.

Next: [Formatting and First Mount](/linux-drives/learn-04-formatting-and-mounting/).
Learn by Examples.4. Formatting and First Mount:
The encrypted volume is open. Now put a filesystem on it and mount it to confirm everything works.

## Format the mapped (decrypted) device

```bash
sudo mkfs.ext4 -L backup_ssd /dev/mapper/backup_ssd
```

```text
Creating filesystem with 122093750 4k blocks and 30531584 inodes
Filesystem UUID: 7c9e4c2a-1234-4abc-8def-0123456789ab
...
Writing superblocks and filesystem accounting information: done
```

Note the label (`backup_ssd`) and take note that a UUID was generated — we'll need it in the next step.

## Create a mount point and mount it

```bash
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/backup_ssd
sudo mount /dev/mapper/backup_ssd /mnt/backup_ssd
```

## Verify

```bash
df -h /mnt/backup_ssd
```

```text
Filesystem                 Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/mapper/backup_ssd     458G   24K  435G   1% /mnt/backup_ssd
```

```bash
lsblk -f /dev/sda
```

```text
NAME             FSTYPE      LABEL       UUID                                 MOUNTPOINTS
sda
└─sda1           crypto_LUKS             a1b2c3d4-5678-90ab-cdef-1234567890ab
  └─backup_ssd   ext4        backup_ssd  7c9e4c2a-1234-4abc-8def-0123456789ab /mnt/backup_ssd
```

Two UUIDs matter here: the **LUKS partition's UUID** (`a1b2c3d4-...` on `sda1`) and the **filesystem's UUID** (`7c9e4c2a-...` on the mapped device). We need both for the next step — persisting this setup across reboots.

## Test write access

```bash
sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) /mnt/backup_ssd
touch /mnt/backup_ssd/test.txt
ls -la /mnt/backup_ssd
```

If that succeeds, the drive is fully functional — encrypted, formatted, mounted, and writable.

Next: [Making It Persistent](/linux-drives/learn-05-making-it-persistent/).
Learn by Examples.5. Making It Persistent:
Right now, everything we did will vanish on reboot — the encrypted volume will be closed and unmounted. Let's make it come back automatically, prompting for the passphrase at boot.

## Get the LUKS partition's UUID

```bash
sudo blkid /dev/sda1
```

```text
/dev/sda1: UUID="a1b2c3d4-5678-90ab-cdef-1234567890ab" TYPE="crypto_LUKS"
```

## Add an entry to /etc/crypttab

```bash
sudo nano /etc/crypttab
```

```text
backup_ssd  UUID=a1b2c3d4-5678-90ab-cdef-1234567890ab  none  luks
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `backup_ssd` | Name to map to (`/dev/mapper/backup_ssd`) — must match what we used with `cryptsetup open` |
| `UUID=...` | The LUKS *partition's* UUID (not the filesystem's) |
| `none` | No keyfile — prompt for a passphrase at boot |
| `luks` | Filesystem type marker for crypttab |

Since this is a removable drive, we'll be asked for the passphrase during boot only if it's plugged in — if it's absent, this line is skipped without blocking startup, as long as we also mark the fstab entry `nofail`.

## Get the filesystem's UUID

```bash
sudo blkid /dev/mapper/backup_ssd
```

```text
/dev/mapper/backup_ssd: LABEL="backup_ssd" UUID="7c9e4c2a-1234-4abc-8def-0123456789ab" TYPE="ext4"
```

## Add an entry to /etc/fstab

```bash
sudo nano /etc/fstab
```

```text
UUID=7c9e4c2a-1234-4abc-8def-0123456789ab  /mnt/backup_ssd  ext4  defaults,noatime,nofail,x-systemd.device-timeout=5  0  2
```

`nofail` matters here — without it, if this removable drive isn't plugged in at boot, the system could hang or drop to a recovery shell waiting for it. `x-systemd.device-timeout=5` caps how long systemd waits for the drive to appear at 5 seconds instead of the 90-second default, so a missing drive doesn't silently add a minute and a half to every boot.

## Test the whole chain without rebooting

Close and remove the current manual setup, then bring it back exactly the way boot would:

```bash
sudo umount /mnt/backup_ssd
sudo cryptsetup close backup_ssd
```

Now replay what crypttab + fstab should do:

```bash
sudo cryptsetup open /dev/sda1 backup_ssd   # simulates the crypttab prompt
sudo mount -a                                # mounts everything in fstab, including our new line
df -h /mnt/backup_ssd
```

If that mounts cleanly, a real reboot will too (you'll just be prompted for the passphrase during boot instead of via this manual command).

Next: [Daily Use](/linux-drives/learn-06-daily-use/).
Learn by Examples.6. Daily Use:
Once persistence is set up, day-to-day interaction with this drive is much simpler than the setup was.

## If it's set up to prompt at boot (crypttab, as above)

Plug it in before booting, or if you plug it in after boot, unlock manually:

```bash
sudo cryptsetup open /dev/sda1 backup_ssd
sudo mount /mnt/backup_ssd
```

(The mount step alone works because `/etc/fstab` already knows the UUID and mount point — you don't need to type the full mount command.)

## Using it

```bash
cp -r ~/Documents /mnt/backup_ssd/
```

## Safely removing it

```bash
sudo umount /mnt/backup_ssd
sudo cryptsetup close backup_ssd
```

Now it's safe to physically unplug.

## Quick status check any time

```bash
lsblk /dev/sda
```

```text
NAME             MAJ:MIN RM   SIZE RO TYPE  MOUNTPOINTS
sda                8:0    1 465.8G  0 disk
└─sda1             8:1    1 465.8G  0 part
  └─backup_ssd   254:0    0 465.8G  0 crypt /mnt/backup_ssd
```

If you see the `crypt` row with a mountpoint, it's unlocked and mounted. No `backup_ssd` row means it's locked (or unplugged).

Next: [Retiring the Drive](/linux-drives/learn-07-retiring-the-drive/).
Learn by Examples.7. Retiring the Drive:
Eventually you might sell this drive, give it away, or just want to wipe it and start over. Here's how to do that safely — encryption actually makes this much easier.

## The easy way: because it's encrypted

If a drive was properly LUKS-encrypted the whole time, you don't need to overwrite every byte to make old data unrecoverable. **Destroying the LUKS header (or all its key slots) makes the encrypted data permanently unreadable**, since the data was never accessible without a key derived through that header.

```bash
sudo umount /mnt/backup_ssd
sudo cryptsetup close backup_ssd
sudo cryptsetup luksErase /dev/sda1
```

```text
This will erase all keyslots on device /dev/sda1.
Are you sure? (Type 'yes' in capital letters): YES
```

At this point, the underlying encrypted data is cryptographically unrecoverable — nobody, including you, can unlock it again. This takes seconds, versus hours for a full-disk overwrite.

## Clean up references

```bash
sudo nano /etc/crypttab    # remove the backup_ssd line
sudo nano /etc/fstab       # remove the backup_ssd line
```

## If you want to fully wipe it anyway (e.g. giving it to someone who shouldn't even see partition structure)

```bash
sudo wipefs -a /dev/sda            # remove all filesystem/partition signatures
sudo dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/sda bs=1M status=progress   # optional: overwrite entirely (slow)
```

For an SSD specifically, a full `dd` overwrite is often unnecessary (and adds wear) — `luksErase` plus `wipefs` is generally sufficient. If the drive supports it and you want to be thorough, a hardware secure-erase is faster and more complete than `dd`:

```bash
sudo pacman -S hdparm
sudo hdparm --user-master u --security-erase p /dev/sda
```

## Final check

```bash
lsblk /dev/sda
sudo blkid /dev/sda
```

No filesystem signatures should be reported — the drive is now ready to repartition from scratch, or hand off.

That's the full lifecycle: identify → partition → encrypt → format → mount → persist → use → retire.
Learn by Examples.Learn by Examples: Overview:
This section follows **one real scenario** end to end: you've plugged in a new 500GB external SSD into your Arch machine and want it as an encrypted, always-available backup drive. We'll go from a completely blank disk to a working, auto-mounting, encrypted volume — then cover how to safely retire it later.

| Page | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| [1. Identifying the New Disk](/linux-drives/learn-01-adding-a-new-disk/) | Find the drive safely among existing ones |
| [2. Partitioning It](/linux-drives/learn-02-partitioning-it/) | Create a GPT table and one partition |
| [3. Encrypting It with LUKS](/linux-drives/learn-03-encrypting-it/) | Turn the partition into an encrypted volume |
| [4. Formatting and First Mount](/linux-drives/learn-04-formatting-and-mounting/) | Put ext4 on it and mount manually |
| [5. Making It Persistent](/linux-drives/learn-05-making-it-persistent/) | crypttab + fstab so it's available (with a prompt) at boot |
| [6. Daily Use](/linux-drives/learn-06-daily-use/) | The two commands you'll actually run day to day |
| [7. Retiring the Drive](/linux-drives/learn-07-retiring-the-drive/) | Safely wiping it before giving it away or discarding it |

Each page assumes you completed the previous one. By the end you'll have used nearly every command from [Essential Commands](/linux-drives/repo-commands-overview/) in a realistic order.

CLI Reference.Identifying disks: lsblk, blkid, fdisk -:
## `lsblk` — list block devices

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-f`, `--fs` | Include filesystem type, label, and UUID |
| `-o COLUMNS` | Choose specific output columns (e.g. `NAME,SIZE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT,UUID`) |
| `-p`, `--paths` | Show full device paths (`/dev/sda1`) instead of bare names |
| `-e MAJ:MIN` | Exclude a device by major:minor number (e.g. exclude loop devices: `-e 7`) |
| `-d`, `--nodeps` | Show only the disks themselves, not their partitions |
| `-J`, `--json` | JSON output |

## `blkid` — identify filesystem/partition attributes

```bash
sudo blkid
sudo blkid /dev/sda1
sudo blkid -s UUID -o value /dev/sda1
```

`-s FIELD` restricts to one field (`UUID`, `TYPE`, `LABEL`, `PARTUUID`); `-o value` prints just the bare value, ideal for capturing into a shell variable or an `fstab` line.

## `fdisk -l` / `parted -l` — list partition tables

```bash
sudo fdisk -l
sudo parted -l
```

Both print every disk's partition table; `parted -l` additionally shows the table type (`gpt`/`msdos`) and partition flags directly without needing a second command.
CLI Reference.Partitioning: fdisk, parted, sgdisk:
## `fdisk` — interactive MBR/GPT editor

```bash
sudo fdisk /dev/sdb
```

Common in-program commands: `n` new partition, `d` delete, `p` print table, `t` change partition type, `w` write and exit, `q` quit without saving, `m` show the help menu, `g` create a new empty GPT table, `o` create a new empty MBR (DOS) table.

## `parted` — scriptable partitioning

```bash
sudo parted /dev/sdb -- mklabel gpt
sudo parted /dev/sdb -- mkpart primary ext4 0% 100%
sudo parted /dev/sdb -- print
sudo parted /dev/sdb -- rm 1
```

| Command | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `mklabel TYPE` | Create a new partition table (`gpt` or `msdos`) |
| `mkpart NAME FS START END` | Create a partition; `%` percentages or units (`MiB`/`GiB`) for bounds |
| `rm NUM` | Delete partition number `NUM` |
| `resizepart NUM END` | Resize a partition's end boundary |
| `set NUM FLAG on\|off` | Toggle a flag (e.g. `boot`, `esp`, `lvm`) |
| `print` | Show the current table |
| `-s`, `--script` | Non-interactive mode, needed when passing commands as CLI arguments (as above) |
| `--align OPT` | Alignment strategy (`optimal`/`minimal`/`none`) |

## `sgdisk` — scriptable GPT-only editor

```bash
sudo sgdisk -n 1:0:+512M -t 1:ef00 /dev/sdb   # EFI system partition
sudo sgdisk -p /dev/sdb                        # print table
```

`-n PART:START:END` creates a partition by number; `-t PART:CODE` sets its GPT type code (`ef00`=EFI System, `8300`=Linux filesystem, `8e00`=Linux LVM).
CLI Reference.Formatting and swap: mkfs, mkswap:
## `mkfs` family

```bash
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1
sudo mkfs.ext4 -L mydata /dev/sdb1
sudo mkfs.xfs -f /dev/sdb1
sudo mkfs.vfat -F 32 /dev/sdb1
sudo mkfs.btrfs -L backup /dev/sdb1
```

| Flag (common across most) | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-L LABEL` | Set a filesystem label at creation time |
| `-f`, `--force` | Force creation even if a filesystem already appears present |
| `-n` | Dry run — show what would happen without writing (ext4: `-n`; xfs: `-N`) |
| `-b SIZE` | Block size in bytes (ext4/xfs) |
| `-F N` | (`mkfs.vfat` only) FAT type: `12`, `16`, or `32` |

## `mkswap` / `swapon` / `swapoff`

```bash
sudo mkswap /dev/sdb2
sudo swapon /dev/sdb2
sudo swapoff /dev/sdb2
swapon --show
```

`mkswap -L LABEL` sets a label; `swapon --show` (or `cat /proc/swaps`) lists active swap devices/files with usage.
CLI Reference.Mounting: mount, umount, fstab options:
## `mount` / `umount`

```bash
sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data
sudo mount -o ro,noexec /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data
sudo mount -a
sudo umount /mnt/data
sudo umount -l /mnt/data
```

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-t TYPE` | Force a filesystem type instead of auto-detecting |
| `-o OPTIONS` | Comma-separated mount options |
| `-a` | Mount everything listed in `/etc/fstab` (skipping already-mounted entries) |
| `-r`, `--read-only` | Shortcut for `-o ro` |
| `-l`, `--lazy` (`umount`) | Detach immediately, clean up once the device stops being busy |
| `-f`, `--force` (`umount`) | Force unmount (risk of data loss on a still-busy device) |

## Common `/etc/fstab` mount options

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `defaults` | `rw,suid,dev,exec,auto,nouser,async` |
| `noatime` / `relatime` | Reduce/limit access-time metadata writes (small performance/SSD-wear win) |
| `ro` / `rw` | Read-only / read-write |
| `noexec` | Disallow executing binaries from this filesystem |
| `nosuid` | Ignore setuid/setgid bits on this filesystem |
| `user` / `nouser` | Allow/disallow non-root users to mount it |
| `auto` / `noauto` | Mount (or don't) automatically at boot / on `mount -a` |
| `nofail` | Don't block boot if this device is missing (essential for removable/optional drives) |
| `x-systemd.automount` | systemd mounts on first access instead of at boot, useful for slow/network drives |
CLI Reference.Encryption, LVM, and repair tools:
## `cryptsetup` (LUKS)

```bash
sudo cryptsetup luksFormat /dev/sdb1
sudo cryptsetup open /dev/sdb1 mydata
sudo cryptsetup close mydata
sudo cryptsetup luksDump /dev/sdb1
sudo cryptsetup luksAddKey /dev/sdb1
```

| Command | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `luksFormat DEVICE` | Initialize LUKS encryption (destroys existing data) |
| `open DEVICE NAME` | Unlock, exposing it at `/dev/mapper/NAME` |
| `close NAME` | Lock it again |
| `luksDump DEVICE` | Show header info and key slots |
| `luksAddKey DEVICE` | Add another passphrase/keyfile slot |
| `luksRemoveKey DEVICE` | Remove a passphrase slot |
| `-c CIPHER` | Cipher spec at format time (default is a strong modern choice; rarely needs changing) |

## LVM: pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate

```bash
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb1
sudo vgcreate myvg /dev/sdb1
sudo lvcreate -L 20G -n mylv myvg
sudo lvextend -L +10G /dev/myvg/mylv
sudo lvs; sudo vgs; sudo pvs
```

| Command | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `pvcreate DEVICE` | Mark a device/partition as an LVM physical volume |
| `vgcreate VGNAME PV...` | Create a volume group from one or more physical volumes |
| `lvcreate -L SIZE -n NAME VG` | Create a logical volume of a fixed size |
| `lvcreate -l 100%FREE -n NAME VG` | Use all remaining free space in the group |
| `lvextend -L +SIZE LV` | Grow a logical volume (pair with `resize2fs`/`xfs_growfs` after) |
| `lvs` / `vgs` / `pvs` | List logical volumes / volume groups / physical volumes |

## Checking and resizing

```bash
sudo fsck /dev/sdb1
sudo e2fsck -f /dev/sdb1
sudo resize2fs /dev/sdb1
sudo xfs_growfs /mnt/data
```

| Command | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `fsck DEVICE` | Filesystem-agnostic check/repair dispatcher |
| `e2fsck -f DEVICE` | Force a full check on an ext2/3/4 filesystem even if it looks clean |
| `resize2fs DEVICE [SIZE]` | Resize an ext2/3/4 filesystem (grow, or shrink with an explicit target size) |
| `xfs_growfs MOUNTPOINT` | Grow an XFS filesystem (XFS can only grow, never shrink, and must be mounted) |
